title: User Authentication
summary: Django authentication: a custom User model built on AbstractUser, DRF token authentication, sign-up, log-in, user-info and log-out endpoints, connecting Axios requests from React to protected views, and linking users to the rest of your models. Step-by-step guide arrives when the lecture is published.
goal: Create a custom Django user model with token log-in and log-out, and protect API views so each user reaches only their own data.

steps.title: Compare Netflix's RLS to Django's approach
steps.detail: In Netflix, anonymous Supabase sign-in gives each visitor a user id, and RLS policies like `(select auth.uid()) = user_id` make the database itself hide other users' rows. Django has no RLS by default: the view reads `request.user` and filters, for example `ListEntry.objects.filter(user=request.user)`.
steps.doneWhen: You can explain in two sentences where "only my rows" is enforced in Supabase (a database policy) and in Django (view code).

steps.title: Read about custom user models
steps.detail: Read "Substituting a custom User model" in Django's auth docs. It explains why you set AUTH_USER_MODEL at the very start of a project.
steps.doneWhen: You can say why the docs want a custom user model from day one.

steps.title: Read DRF token authentication
steps.detail: Read the TokenAuthentication section of the DRF authentication guide.
steps.doneWhen: You can write the header a client sends: `Authorization: Token <key>`.

concepts.meaning: Django's base user class you extend to make your own User model.
The server gives the user a random key at log-in; the client sends it with every request.
The logged-in user Django attaches to each request (or AnonymousUser).
Authentication is who you are; authorization is what you're allowed to do.
A DRF rule, like IsAuthenticated, that decides whether a request may reach a view.
